title: Voynich Manuscript: Still Unreadable, But What Has Research Revealed?
description:
How did a book in a dealer's hands reach the lab? We follow its purchase, parchment dating, text statistics, a university statement in 2019, and multispectral images revisited in 2024, before examining the author's 2025 Naibbe model. The parchment's age, later marginal notes, and statistically similar generated text each answer different questions. None amounts to reading the original manuscript.

Fact checked: 2026-10-16. The Naibbe segment relies on the author's README; we do not claim to have rerun the model or read the restricted full paper. AI illustrations are narrative aids; on-screen words and process diagrams were added in postproduction. Living researchers are not shown as recognizable portraits.

chapters.model-new: Can a model make similar text?

va7e787b.text: Italy, 1912. A bookseller buys a book. Inside: plants and unfamiliar writing.

v3962cb5.text: The pictures hint at meaning. The lines beside them have no agreed reading.

v1687a61.text: Later, researchers take a tiny sample of the parchment to ask how old it is.

v766e7f7.text: A university announces a proposed reading. Scholars soon raise doubts.

v960e564.text: Later, images shot in varied light are reprocessed to see faded margin notes.

v98729cd.text: Can these methods reveal the text, or answer different questions first?

vc14d268.text: Voynich tries to decode the book until he dies. He never solves its mystery.

vde0982c.text: Earlier readers left traces on those pages. Researchers seek clues in the book.

v8949601.text: Today's library catalog lists 102 parchment leaves, including foldouts.

v2405e28.text: A leaf has two sides. So a count of leaves is not a page count.

vd5e8190.text: A plant may fill a page, with lines beside it that seem to explain it.

v179b9a8.text: But until we can read them, we cannot know if they describe the plant's use.

v61e210f.text: Turn the page and the images change: star shapes and connected circular designs.

v339ff28.text: The drawings split the book into sections, but do not give us a dictionary.

v44daffa.text: With author and script unknown, researchers record visible shapes to compare.

vaa3669c.text: Later readers added margin notes. Separate traces from different periods before studying the text.

v524a452.text: If we cannot read a sentence, can we start with its material?

v57b521e.text: Remember that tiny sample? To date it, researchers turn to the parchment.

v5f9aa2e.text: Conservators chose unrepaired areas before letting the lab take samples.

v0e564e3.text: Researchers took one thin strip from each of four leaves: four samples in all.

v771b973.text: They clean the samples first: finger oils or binding glue could skew dates.

vd7a16ea.text: Parchment is animal skin. Carbon absorbed during life helps date it.

v611e63e.text: The lab dates the material. Translating its words is another question.

v9b3074b.text: The 2009 dating work placed the material in the early fifteenth century.

vcbef25e.text: That result dates the parchment, not the moment each ink stroke was written.

v4a9a901.text: Dating the ink itself is hard: enough material must be taken and kept separate.

v3be0bcb.text: Researchers still had to open the book and record its recurring letter shapes.

v652f3b2.text: Even before we know their meaning, could the words' positions offer a clue?

va099beb.text: They compare forms that cluster together and forms in certain book sections.

v2fc22c8.text: Instead of asking what one sign resembles, they map how the whole text spreads.

v4394559.text: A 2013 study used information theory to analyze that distribution.

v16d9e2d.text: They used an existing transcription, assigning fixed symbols to count words.

v6856059.text: They split the text evenly and compared each part's words and their counts.

ve1179dc.text: A word marks a section if common there, but not if it appears everywhere.

va919cc7.text: Some words cluster in one section; other words dominate the next.

vfc824ec.text: They compared Shiji in Chinese, On the Origin of Species in English, and Latin texts.

va972623.text: What about those plant drawings? Could the text alone link related sections?

vd262f61.text: Word patterns alone linked two plant-heavy sections, echoing the images.

va085d00.text: Authors compared it with known languages and saw signs of linguistic structure.

v404103f.text: Some clustered words share opening or closing shapes, inviting closer study.

v98e1b79.text: But clustering words still cannot tell us which plant a passage describes.

v361508d.text: When someone later claims to read the book, will other researchers accept it?

v14ba199.text: In 2019, Bristol publicized an honorary researcher's paper on the manuscript.

v7639780.text: The paper had appeared in Romance Studies after double-blind peer review.

va5b5d45.text: Linguists and medieval scholars raised doubts about the study's validity.

vd9827f1.text: On May 16, the next day, the university issued a statement.

vec5b307.text: It said he did the research independently; the university had not participated.

v470a2c5.text: After those doubts, the university removed its news release pending checks.

vc25d396.text: The news release was removed; that alone does not mean the paper was retracted.

v438a4b9.text: The book remained in the collection, its faint margin marks outlasting headlines.

v07a5163.text: Could those marks reveal a clue left by another reader?

v2b32364.text: In 2024, earlier images led researchers back to the manuscript.

v3763f90.text: Taken ten years earlier, they used different wavelengths to examine ten pages.

vd854ca2.text: Light may change how ink and parchment appear, making faint strokes clearer.

v7cc1054.text: Some details were known; now the full image set and new processing were released.

vaee9829.text: Clearer images can mislead. Pale blue marks appeared on a page. Hidden text?

v1df5834.text: Davis reversed the image, checked the leaf's back, and found show-through text.

v965353b.text: The opening search now points to columns of marks on the first page's right margin.

v81627c3.text: Davis found three columns: Latin letters, manuscript signs, then Latin again.

v173f6fc.text: A green leaf image on the back obscured the edge. Davis asked an imaging expert to reveal more.

v0931109.text: The Latin columns are offset by one position, as if aligning symbols.

vc34e31d.text: Davis compared the marks with handwriting by earlier handlers of the manuscript.

v439465f.text: Davis saw traits of Marci's handwriting in the margin; her reading is tentative.

v4353a57.text: The columns' purpose is unsettled. They offer no key to read the whole book.

v7cfdf05.text: What of those earlier text patterns? If similar writing can be made, what do they tell us?

v2ebbd0d.text: In 2025, researcher Greshko offered a different approach: a model called Naibbe.

v199620f.text: It had to be done by hand using fifteenth-century materials.

v37a7ba4.text: It starts with known Latin or Italian, then transforms it by set steps.

v2a16849.text: Greshko says its output shares several statistical features with the manuscript.

vb393dd6.text: It offers a possible way to make such text, but does not translate the original.

vd56bdd7.text: Known input lets us read the model's output. The original still lacks a verified reading.

v6911d5a.text: Remember the book? Its parchment and margins give clues; its text still needs a testable reading.

v75e1ebb.text: What would you examine first: images, writing, or parchment?

v9e503a3.text: Subscribe and help us trace strange stories through verifiable records.
